page_title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 5: Addresses - Going the distance

summary.title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 5: Addresses
summary.one_liner: You learn how Bitcoin-style addresses are derived from ECDSA public keys (SHA256, RIPEMD160, checksum, Base58) and how transactions are signed and verified in a toy Go blockchain.
keywords: public key vs private key bitcoin
takeaways: A Bitcoin address is a Base58 encoding of version + RIPEMD160(SHA256(PubKey)) + a 4-byte double-SHA256 checksum.
Wallets are ECDSA key pairs on the P-256 curve; the public key is the concatenated X and Y coordinates.
Transaction signatures cover a trimmed copy of the transaction: referenced output public key hashes, new output hashes and values, not the input public keys.
Inputs store raw public keys and signatures; outputs store only the public key hash, and verification checks both the hash match and the signature.
summary.summary: The article explains why Bitcoin uses addresses instead of user accounts, covering public-key cryptography, digital signatures, elliptic curves (ECDSA) and Base58 encoding. It then implements these in Go: a Wallet type that generates key pairs, an address function that hashes and checksums the public key, and output locking and input unlocking helpers that replace the earlier arbitrary-string addresses. Finally it shows how transactions are signed over a trimmed copy and verified against previous outputs before mining, with command-line examples of creating wallets and sending coins.
